name: Balsam of Peru

card.summary: A fragrant tree resin used in perfumes, cosmetics and folk skin remedies, and the standard patch-test marker for fragrance allergy, which matters to anyone with skin that reacts to products.
card.aka: Myroxylon pereirae, Peru balsam, Balsam of Tolu (related)
card.note: A common contact allergen; listed as Myroxylon pereirae on cosmetic labels.

quick.overview:
Balsam of Peru is a dark, aromatic resin from the tree Myroxylon balsamum var. pereirae, used as a flavoring, a fragrance and an ingredient in some topical and dental products. In skin care it is best known as a marker for fragrance allergy: people whose skin reacts to scented products are often patch-tested with it.

Its appearance relevance is therefore mostly about avoiding irritated, red, eczematous skin. Dermatology reviews list it among the most common fragrance screening allergens, alongside fragrance mix 1 and 2.
quick.how: In practice, people with suspected fragrance allergy have it applied in a dermatologist's patch test, and those who test positive choose products labelled free of Myroxylon pereirae and sometimes review diet for related flavorings, such as spices, citrus and tomato.
quick.risks: It can cause allergic contact dermatitis, lip and mouth inflammation, hand eczema and other reactions. Crude balsam was banned as a fragrance ingredient by the International Fragrance Association in 1982, and a 2006 European Commission opinion allowed extracts and distillates up to 0.4%.

lead: Balsam of Peru is a resin-like balsam from the tree Myroxylon balsamum var. pereirae, native to Central and South America. It is used as a flavoring, a fragrance and an ingredient in medicinal products such as toothpastes and wound sprays [1]. The name is a misnomer: the balsam was collected in Central America and shipped through Callao, Peru, en route to Europe [1].

For looks, its significance lies in skin reactivity. Balsam of Peru is one of the most common fragrance screeners in baseline patch-test series, with fragrance mix 1 and 2, because fragrance allergy affects roughly 0.7% to 2.6% of the general population and 5% to 11% of patch-tested patients [2]. Identifying it helps people with recurring facial or hand dermatitis avoid products that trigger it.

chain: Patch test identifies balsam of Peru allergy
Fewer eczema flares and calmer skin
angle.text: It is not a product people apply to look better. Its role is as a diagnostic marker: knowing about the allergy lets someone choose cosmetics and fragrances that do not provoke rashes, redness and lip inflammation.

infobox: Cinnamein, cinnamic acid, benzyl benzoate, vanillin [1]
Flavoring, fragrance, topical and dental products
Crude balsam banned as fragrance by IFRA, 1982 [1]

paras: The balsam is collected by stripping bark so the tree exudes resin, which is soaked into rags, boiled and separated from the water to give a dark oily liquid [1]. It contains about 25 substances, including cinnamein, cinnamic acid, benzyl benzoate and vanillin, plus a large fraction of resins of unknown composition [1].

It flavors coffee, alcoholic beverages, sodas, sauces and sweets, scents perfumes, cosmetics and toiletries, and appears in toothpaste, wound sprays, candles and some cleaning products [1]. It is often hidden under generic labels such as fragrance, which makes it hard to spot [1].

It is among the top five allergens behind positive patch tests, and a 2001 study found 3.8% of the general population tested was allergic [1]. A 2020 dermatology review lists it among the most common fragrance screeners and notes that supplemental fragrance or essential oil series can aid diagnosis [2]. Reactions include contact dermatitis, mouth and lip inflammation, hand eczema, rhinitis and conjunctivitis [1].

People with the allergy may be advised to avoid foods containing it, most often spices, citrus and tomatoes [1]. A review of systemic contact dermatitis describes eruptions that follow systemic exposure to an allergen [3].

European export was first documented in the 17th century, and the balsam is now exported mainly from El Salvador [1]. Before 1977 it was the main recommended perfume allergy marker [1]. The International Fragrance Association banned crude balsam as a fragrance compound in 1982, and a March 2006 European Commission opinion permitted extracts and distillates up to 0.4% [1].
Patch-test studies and reviews report its prevalence as an allergen [1][2]. No trials have tested it as a treatment for skin appearance.
